{{Short description|Use of mathematical groups in magnetochemistry}}
[[File:Frobenius_character_tables_binary_subgroups_1899.pdf|thumb|upright=1|The character tables of the binary tetrahedral, octahedral and icosahedral groups following [[Georg Frobenius|Frobenius]] (1899)<ref name=Frobenius>{{cite journal|year=1899|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/93034#page/378/mode/1up |pages = 330–339 | language = de
|first= F. G. |last = Frobenius| author-link=Georg Frobenius|journal= Sitzungsberichte der Königlich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin |title=Über die Composition der Charaktere einer Gruppe|volume=Jan-Juni 1899 }}</ref>]]

In [[applied mathematics]], finite subgroups of the [[special unitary group]] {{math|SU(2)}} are [[Group (mathematics)|groups]] composed of rotations and related transformations, employed particularly in the field of [[physical chemistry]]. The [[symmetry group]] of a [[physical body]] generally contains a [[subgroup]] (typically finite) of the [[3D rotation group]]. It may occur that the group {{math|{{mset|±1}}}} with two elements acts also on the body; this is typically the case in [[magnetism]] for the exchange of north and south poles, or in [[quantum mechanics]] for the change of [[spin (physics)|spin]] sign. In this case, the symmetry group of a body may be a [[central extension (mathematics)|central extension]] of the group of spatial symmetries by the group with two elements. [[Hans Bethe]] introduced the term "[[double group]]" (''Doppelgruppe'') for such a group, in which two different elements induce the spatial identity, and a rotation of {{math|2''π''}} may correspond to an element of the double group that is not the identity.

The classification of the finite double groups and their [[character table]]s is therefore physically meaningful and is thus the main part of the theory of double groups. Finite double groups include the [[binary polyhedral group]]s.

In physical chemistry, double groups are used in the treatment of the [[magnetochemistry]] of [[Coordination complex|complexes]] of metal ions that have a single unpaired electron in the d-shell or f-shell.<ref name="cotton">{{cite book |last1=Cotton |first1=F. Albert|author1-link=F. Albert Cotton |title=Chemical Applications of Group Theory |date=1971 |publisher=Wiley |location=New York |isbn=0-471-17570-6 |pages=289–294, 376}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Tsukerblat |first1=Boris S. |title=Group Theory in Chemistry and Spectroscopy |date=2006 |publisher=Dover Publications Inc. |location=Mineola, New York |isbn=0-486-45035-X |pages=245–253}}</ref> Instances when a double group is commonly used include 6-coordinate complexes of [[copper]](II), [[titanium]](III) and [[cerium]](III). In these double groups rotation by 360° is treated as a symmetry operation separate from the identity operation; the double group is formed by combining these two symmetry operations with a [[point group]] such as a [[Dihedral symmetry in three dimensions|dihedral group]] or the [[Octahedral symmetry#Full octahedral symmetry|full octahedral group]].

== Definition and theory ==
Let {{math|''Γ''}} be a finite subgroup of [[SO(3)]], the three-dimensional rotation group. There is a natural homomorphism {{mvar|f}} of [[SU(2)]] onto SO(3) which has kernel {{math|{{mset|±I}}}}.{{sfn|Wigner|1959}} This [[double cover (topology)|double cover]] can be realised using the [[adjoint action]] of SU(2) on its [[Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{su}(2)</math> of traceless 2-by-2 [[Skew-Hermitian matrix|skew-adjoint]] matrices or using the action by conjugation of [[unit quaternions]]. The '''double group''' {{math|''Γ''{{′}}}} is defined as {{math|''f''<sup>−1</sup>(''Γ'')}}. By construction, {{mset|±I}} is a [[central subgroup]] of {{math|''Γ''{{′}}}} and the quotient is isomorphic to {{mvar|Γ}}. Thus {{math|''Γ''{{′}}}} is a [[Group extension#central extension|central extension]] of the group {{math|''Γ''}} by {{mset|±1}}, the [[cyclic group]] of order 2. Ordinary representations of {{math|''Γ''{{′}}}} are just mappings of {{mvar|Γ}} into the [[general linear group]] that are homomorphisms up to a sign; equivalently, they are [[projective representation]]s of {{mvar|Γ}} with a [[factor system]] or [[Schur multiplier]] in {{mset|±1}}. Two projective representations of {{mvar|Γ}} are closed under the tensor product operation, with their corresponding factor systems in {{mset|±1}} multiplying. The central extensions of {{math|''Γ''}} by {{mset|±1}} also have a natural product.{{sfn|Bethe|1929}}

The finite subgroups of SU(2) and SO(3) were determined in 1876 by [[Felix Klein]] in an article in ''[[Mathematische Annalen]]'', later incorporated in his celebrated 1884 "Lectures on the Icosahedron": for SU(2), the subgroups correspond to the cyclic groups, the [[binary dihedral group]]s, the [[binary tetrahedral group]], the [[binary octahedral group]], and the [[binary icosahedral group]]; and for SO(3), they correspond to the cyclic groups, the [[dihedral group]]s, the [[tetrahedral group]], the [[octahedral group]] and the [[icosahedral group]]. The correspondence can be found in numerous text books, and goes back to the classification of [[platonic solids]]. From Klein's classifications of binary subgroups, it follows that, if {{math|''Γ''}} a finite subgroup of SO(3), then, up to equivalence, there are exactly two central extensions of {{mvar|Γ}} by {{mset|±1}}: the one obtained by lifting the double cover {{math|1=''Γ''{{′}} = ''f''<sup>−1</sup>(''Γ'')}}; and the trivial extension {{math|''Γ'' × {{mset|±1}}}}.{{sfn|Bethe|1929}}<ref name=Griffith/><ref name=Ramond/><ref name=Jacobs/><ref name=Wolf>{{cite book|mr=0217740|last=Wolf|first= Joseph A.|author-link=Joseph Wolf|title=Spaces of constant curvature|publisher= [[McGraw-Hill]]|location= New York-London-Sydney|year= 1967|pages=83–88}}</ref>

The [[character table]]s of the finite subgroups of SU(2) and SO(3) were determined and tabulated by [[Georg Frobenius|F. G. Frobenius]] in 1898,<ref name=Frobenius /> with alternative derivations by [[Issai Schur|I. Schur]] and H. E. Jordan in 1907 independently. [[Restricted representation|Branching rules]] and [[tensor product of representations|tensor product formulas]] were also determined. For each binary subgroup, i.e. finite subgroup of SU(2), the [[irreducible representation]]s of {{math|''Γ''}} are labelled by [[affine Dynkin diagram|extended Dynkin diagrams]] of type A, D and E; the rules for tensoring with the two-dimensional vector representation are given graphically by an [[McKay graph|undirected graph]].<ref name=Griffith/><ref name=Ramond/><ref name=Jacobs/> By [[Schur's lemma]], irreducible representations of {{math|''Γ'' × {{mset|±1}}}} are just irreducible representations of {{math|''Γ''}} multiplied by either the trivial or the sign character of {{math|{{mset|±1}}}}. Likewise, irreducible representations of {{math|''Γ''{{′}}}} that send {{math|−1}} to {{math|''I''}} are just ordinary representations of {{math|''Γ''}}; while those which send {{math|−1}} to {{math|−''I''}} are genuinely double-valued or spinor representations.{{sfn|Bethe|1929}}

'''Example.''' The tensor product rules for tensoring with the two-dimensional representation are encoded diagrammatically below:

[[File:Affine E8 diagram.svg|thumb|left|500px]]
{{clear}}

The numbering has at the top <math>\chi_{3^\prime}</math> and then below, from left to right, <math>\chi_{2^\prime}^*</math>, <math>\chi_{4}</math>, <math>\chi_6^*</math>, <math>\chi_{5}</math>, <math>\chi_4^*</math>, <math>\chi_{3}</math>, <math>\chi_2^*</math>, and <math>\chi_{1}</math>. Thus, on labelling the vertices by irreducible characters, the result of multiplying <math>\chi_2^*</math> by a given irreducible character equals the sum of all irreducible characters labelled by an adjacent vertex.{{sfn|Ramond|2010}}

The [[representation theory of SU(2)]] goes back to the nineteenth century and the theory of invariants of binary forms, with the figures of [[Alfred Clebsch]] and [[Paul Gordan]] prominent.<ref name=WeylClassical>{{cite book|mr=0000255 |last=Weyl|first= Hermann|author-link=Hermann Weyl| edition=2nd| year=1946|title= [[The Classical Groups]]. Their Invariants and Representations|publisher= [[Princeton University Press]]|isbn= 0-691-05756-7| series = Princeton Landmarks in Mathematics}} [https://archive.org/details/classicalgroups02edunse/page/n5/mode/2up Archive], [https://www-fourier.ujf-grenoble.fr/~panchish/ETE%20LAMA%202018-AP/Weyl_The%20Classical%20Groups.pdf Institut Fourier]</ref><ref name=Wigner1959 /><ref name=WeylQuantum>{{cite book|jfm=54.0954.03 |last=Weyl| first= Hermann|title=The theory of groups and quantum mechanics [Gruppentheorie und Quantenmechanik]|edition= Second revised|translator= H. P. Robertson|publisher= [[Dover Books]]|location= New York|year= 1950}} First edition in 1928 from notes of [[John von Neumann|von Neumann]]; second edition (in German), expanded and simplified in 1931.</ref><ref>{{cite book|mr=0479090 |last1=van der Waerden|first1= B. L.|author1-link=B. L. van der Waerden| title=Group theory and quantum mechanics (translated from the 1932 German original)|series= Die Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften|volume= 214|publisher= [[Springer-Verlag]]|location= New York-Heidelberg|year= 1974}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|mr = 0198828 |last=Tinkham|first= Michael|author-link=Michael Tinkham|
title=Group Theory and Quantum Mechanics|publisher= [[McGraw-Hill]]| year=1964}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Cracknell|first= Arthur P.

Ja.| title=Special functions and the theory of group representations|translator= V. N. Singh|series= Translations of Mathematical Monographs|volume= 22 |publisher= [[American Mathematical Society]]|location= Providence|year= 1968}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Želobenko|first= D. P.|title=Compact Lie groups and their representations|series=Translations of Mathematical Monographs|volume=40|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|year= 1973}}</ref> The irreducible representations of SU(2) are indexed by non-negative half integers {{mvar|j}}. If {{mvar|V}} is the two-dimensional vector representation, then {{mvar|V<sub>j</sub>}} = S<sup>2''j''</sup> {{mvar|V}}, the {{math|2''j''}}th [[symmetric power]] of {{mvar|V}}, a {{math|(2''j'' + 1)}}-dimensional vector space. Letting {{var|G}} be the compact group SU(2), the group {{mvar|G}} acts irreducibly on each {{mvar|V<sub>j</sub>}} and satisfies the Clebsch-Gordan rules:
: <math>V_i \otimes V_j \cong V_{|i-j|} \oplus V_{|i-j|+1} \oplus \cdots \oplus V_{i+j -1} \oplus V_{i+j}.</math>

In particular <math> V_j \otimes V_{{1\over 2}} \cong V_{j-{1\over 2}} \oplus V_{j+{1\over 2}}</math> for {{mvar|j}} > 0, and <math>V_0 \otimes V_{{1\over 2}} \cong  V_{{1\over 2}}.</math> By definition, the matrix representing {{mvar|g}} in {{mvar|V<sub>j</sub>}} is just S<sup>2''j''</sup> ( {{mvar|g}} ). Since every {{mvar|g}} is conjugate to a diagonal matrix with diagonal entries <math>\zeta</math> and <math>\zeta^{-1}</math> (the order being immaterial), in this case S<sup>2''j''</sup> ( {{mvar|g}} ) has diagonal entries <math>\zeta^{2j}</math>, <math>\zeta^{2j-1}</math>, ... , <math>\zeta^{-2j+1}</math>, <math>\zeta^{-2j}</math>. Setting <math>\pi_j(g) =S^{2j}(g),</math> this yields the character formula
: <math>\chi_j(g) := {\rm Tr} \, \pi_j(g) = \sum_{k=-2j}^{2j} \zeta^k = {\zeta^{2j+1} - \zeta^{-2j-1}\over \zeta -\zeta^{-1}}.</math>

Substituting <math>\zeta =e^{i\alpha/2}</math>, it follows that, if {{mvar|g}} has diagonal entries <math>e^{\pm i\alpha/2},</math> then
: <math>\chi_j(g) = {\sin (j + {1/2})\alpha  \over \sin \alpha/2}.</math>

The representation theory of SU(2), including that of SO(3), can be developed in many different ways:{{sfn|Weyl|1946}}
* using the complexification ''G''<sub>c</sub> = [[SL(2,C)]] and the double coset decomposition ''G''<sub>c</sub> = ''B'' ⋅ ''w'' ⋅ ''B''  ∐  ''B'', where ''B'' denotes upper triangular matrices and <math>w = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}</math>;
* using the infinitesimal action of the Lie algebras of SU(2) and SL(2,C) where they appear as raising and lowering operators {{mvar|E}}, {{mvar|F}}, {{mvar|H}} of [[angular momentum operator|angular momentum]] in [[quantum mechanics]]: here ''E''  = <math>\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}</math>, ''F'' = ''E''* and ''H'' = [''E'', ''F''] so that [''H'', ''E''] = 2''E'' and [''H'', ''F''] = −2''F'';
* using integration of [[class function]]s over SU(2), identifying the unit quaternions with 3-sphere and [[Haar measure]] as the volume form: this reduces to integration over the diagonal matrices, i.e. the circle group '''T'''.

The properties of [[matrix coefficient]]s or [[representative function]]s of the compact group SU(2) (and SO(3)) are well documented as part of the theory of special functions:{{sfn|Vilenkin|1968}}{{sfn|Želobenko|1973}} the [[Casimir operator]] {{math|1=''C'' = ''H''<sup>2</sup> + 2''EF'' + 2''FE''}} commutes with the Lie algebras and groups. The operator {{math|{{sfrac|1|4}}''C''}} can be identified with the Laplacian {{math|Δ}}, so that on a matrix coefficient {{mvar|φ}} of {{math|''V''<sub>''j''</sub>}}, {{math|1=Δ''φ'' = (''j''<sup>2</sup> + ''j'')''φ''}}.

The representative functions {{mvar|A}} form a non-commutative algebra under [[convolution]] with respect to Haar measure {{mvar|μ}}.  The analogue for a finite subgroup of {{mvar|Γ}} of SU(2) is the finite-dimensional group algebra '''C'''[{{mvar|Γ}}]  From the Clebsch-Gordan rules, the convolution algebra {{mvar|A}} is isomorphic to a direct sum of {{math|''n'' × ''n''}} matrices, with {{math|1=''n'' = 2''j'' + 1}} and {{math|''j'' ≥ 0}}. The matrix coefficients for each irreducible representation {{math|''V''<sub>''j''</sub>}} form a set of [[matrix unit]]s. This direct sum decomposition is the [[Peter-Weyl theorem]]. The corresponding result for '''C'''[{{math|''Γ''}}] is [[Maschke's theorem]]. The algebra {{math|''A''}} has eigensubspaces {{math|1=''a''(''gζ'') = ''a''(''g'')}} or {{math|''a''(''g'')''ζ''}}, exhibiting them as direct sum of {{math|''V''<sub>''j''</sub>}}, summed over {{mvar|j}} non-negative integers or positive half-integers – these are examples of [[induced representation]]s. It allows the computations of branching rules from SU(2) to {{math|''Γ''}}, so that {{math|''V''<sub>''j''</sub>}} can be decomposed as direct sums of irreducible representations of {{mvar|Γ}}.{{sfn|Hochschild|1965}}{{sfn|Griffith|1961}}{{sfn|Vilenkin|1968}}{{sfn|Ramond|2010}}

== History ==
[[Georg Frobenius]] derived and listed in 1899 the [[character table]]s of the finite subgroups of [[SU(2)]], the double cover of the rotation group [[SO(3)]]. In 1875, [[Felix Klein]] had already classified these finite "binary" subgroups into the [[cyclic group]]s, the [[binary dihedral group]]s, the [[binary tetrahedral group]], the [[binary octahedral group]] and the [[binary icosahedral group]]. Alternative derivations of the character tables were given by [[Issai Schur]] and H.&nbsp;E.&nbsp;Jordan in 1907; further [[Restricted representation|branching rules]] and [[tensor product of representations|tensor product formulas]] were also determined.<ref name="Griffith">{{cite book|first=J. S.|last=Griffith|author-link=John Stanley Griffith|title=The Theory of Transition-Metal Ions|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]| url= https://archive.org/details/theoryoftransiti0000grif_n9d2|year=1961|isbn=9780521115995}}</ref><ref name="Ramond">{{cite book|mr=2663568 |last=Ramond|first= Pierre | author-link=Pierre Ramond|title=Group theory. A physicist's survey|publisher= [[Cambridge University Press]]|year=2010| isbn= 978-0-521-89603-0}}</ref><ref name="Jacobs">{{cite book| first=Patrick|last=Jacobs|doi=10.1017/CBO9780511535390
|title=Group Theory with Applications in Chemical Physics|year=2005 |isbn=9780511535390|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]}}</ref>

In a 1929 article on splitting of atoms in crystals, the [[physics|physicist]] [[Hans Bethe|H. Bethe]] first coined the term "double group" (''Doppelgruppe''),<ref name="Bethe">{{cite journal |last1=Bethe |first1=Hans|author1-link = Hans Bethe |title=Termaufspaltung in Kristallen |trans-title=Splitting of Terms in Crystals|language=de|journal=[[Annalen der Physik]] |date=1929 |volume=395| issue=3 |pages=133–206 |doi=10.1002/andp.19293950202 |bibcode=1929AnP...395..133B | url = https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k15392p/f141.item|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>English translation in {{cite book|title=Selected Works of Hans A. Bethe with commentary|first=Hans|last=Bethe|translator=Hans Bethe|publisher= [[World Scientific]]|pages=1–72|isbn=9789810228767|year=1996}} Bethe's commentary: "If an atom is placed in a crystal, its energy levels are split. The splitting depends on the symmetry of the location of the atom in the crystal. The splitting is derived here from group theory. This paper has been widely used, especially by physical chemists."</ref> a concept that allowed [[projective representation|double-valued or spinor representations]] of finite subgroups of the rotation group to be regarded as ordinary linear representations of their double covers.{{efn|In his 1931 book ''Gruppentheorie und ihre Anwendung auf die Quantenmechanik der Atomspektren'',<ref name=Wigner1931>{{cite book|language=de|first=Eugen|last= Wigner|author-link=Eugene Wigner|
title=Gruppentheorie und ihre Anwendung auf die Quantenmechanik der Atomspektren|year=1931|isbn=9783663025559|publisher=[[Vieweg+Teubner Verlag]]|url=https://digbib.ubka.uni-karlsruhe.de/volltexte/wasbleibt/33355459/33355459.pdf}}</ref><ref name=Wigner1959>{{cite book|mr=0106711|last=Wigner|first= Eugene| title=Group theory and its application to the quantum mechanics of atomic spectra|edition=Expanded and improved|translator= J. J. Griffin|series= Pure and Applied Physics|volume= 5|publisher=[[Academic Press]]|location= New York–London|year=1959|page=157}}</ref> [[Eugene Wigner]] describes in detail how SU(2) arises as a double cover of SO(3), following [[Hermann Weyl]]. Referring to a 1928 article of [[John von Neumann|von Neumann]] and Wigner in [[Zeitschrift für Physik]] (vol. 49), {{harvtxt|Bethe|1929}} explains why double-valued representations of finite groups are involved.}}{{efn|In mathematical language, a double group Γ′ is defined to be a [[Group extension#central extension|central extension]] of the group Γ by {{mset|±1}}, the [[cyclic group]] of order 2: thus ordinary representations of Γ′ are just mappings of Γ into the [[general linear group]] that are homomorphisms up to a sign; equivalently, they are [[projective representation]]s of Γ with a [[factor system]] or [[Schur multiplier]] in {{mset|±1}}.}} In particular, Bethe applied his theory to [[relativistic quantum mechanics]] and [[crystallographic point group]]s, where a natural [[crystallographic restriction theorem|physical restriction]] to 32 point groups occurs. Subsequently, the non-crystallographic icosahedral case has also been investigated more extensively, resulting most recently in groundbreaking advances on [[carbon 60]] and [[fullerenes]] in the 1980s and 90s.<ref>{{cite book|mr=1327532|last1=Chung|first1= Fan R. K.|author1-link=Fan Chung|last2= Kostant|first2= Bertram| author2-link= Bertram Kostant| last3=Sternberg|first3= Shlomo |author3-link= Shlomo Sternberg|year=1994|chapter=Groups and the buckyball|title= Lie theory and geometry|pages= 97–126|series=Progress in Mathematics|volume= 123|publisher=[[Birkhäuser]]|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-0261-5_4 |isbn=978-1-4612-6685-3 |
chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-1-4612-0261-5_4}} {{subscription required}}</ref><ref>{{cite book| mr=1314673 |last=Yang|first =C. N.|author-link=C. N. == Applications ==
=== Magnetochemistry ===
In magnetochemistry, the need for a double group arises in a very particular circumstance, namely, in the treatment of the magnetic properties of complexes of a metal ion in whose electronic structure there is a single unpaired electron (or its equivalent, a single vacancy) in a metal ion's d- or f- shell. This occurs, for example, with the elements [[copper]], [[silver]] and [[gold]] in the +2 oxidation state, where there is a single vacancy in the d-electron shell, with [[titanium]](III) which has a single electron in the 3d shell and with [[cerium]](III) which has a single electron in the 4f shell.

In [[group theory]], the [[Character (mathematics)|character]] <math>\chi</math>, for rotation, by an angle {{math|''α''}}, of a wavefunction for half-integer angular momentum is given by
: <math>\chi^J (\alpha) = \frac{\sin [J+1/2] \alpha } {\sin  (1/2) \alpha }</math>
where angular momentum is the [[vector sum]] of spin and orbital momentum, {{math|1=''J'' = ''L'' + ''S''}}. This formula applies with angular momentum in general.

In atoms with a single unpaired electron the character for a rotation through an angle of {{math|2''π'' + ''α''}} is equal to <math>-\chi^J (\alpha)</math>. The change of sign cannot be true for an identity operation in any point group. Therefore, a double group, in which rotation by {{math|2''π''}} is classified as being distinct from the identity operation, is used. 
A character table for the double group D<sub>4</sub>′ is as follows. The new operation is labelled R in this example.
The character table for the point group D<sub>4</sub> is shown for comparison.

Character tables for the double groups T′,  O′, T<sub>d</sub>′, D<sub>3h</sub>′, C<sub>6v</sub>′, D<sub>6</sub>′, D<sub>2d</sub>′, C<sub>4v</sub>′, D<sub>4</sub>′, C<sub>3v</sub>′, D<sub>3</sub>′, C<sub>2v</sub>′, D<sub>2</sub>′ and R(3)′ are given in {{harvtxt|Koster|Dimmock|Wheeler|Statz|1963}}, {{harvtxt|Salthouse|Ware|1972}} and {{harvtxt|Cornwell|1984}}.<ref name=sw>{{cite book |last1=Salthouse |first1=J.A. |last2=Ware |first2=M.J. |title=Point group character tables and related data |date=1972 |publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] |location=Cambridge |isbn=0-521-081394 |pages=55–57}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|mr =0159664 |last1=Koster|first1= George F.|last2= Dimmock|first2= John O.|last3= Wheeler|first3=Robert G.|last4= Statz|first4= Hermann|title =Properties of the thirty-two point groups|publisher= [[The M.I.T. Press]]|location= Cambridge, Mass.|year= 1963}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|mr = 0751778 | last= Cornwell| first= J. F. | title = Group theory in physics. Vol. I| publisher= [[Academic Press]]| year= 1984| isbn= 0-12-189801-6|pages=342–355|chapter=The double crystallographic point groups}}</ref>{{efn|R(3)′ refers to [[SU(2)]], the double cover of the three-dimensional rotation group [[SO(3)]]}}
[[image:Octahedral-3D-balls.png|thumb|150px|left|Sub-structure at the center of an octahedral complex]]
[[image:Square-planar-3D-balls.png|thumb|170px|Structure of a square-planar complex ion such as {{bracket|AgF<sub>4</sub>}}<sup>2−</sup>]]
[[Image:Endohedral fullerene.png|thumb|170px|An atom or ion (red) held in a C<sub>60</sub> fullerene cage]]
The need for a double group occurs, for example, in the treatment of [[Magnetochemistry|magnetic properties]] of 6-coordinate complexes of [[copper]](II). The electronic configuration of the central Cu<sup>2+</sup> ion can be written as [Ar]3d<sup>9</sup>. It can be said that there is a single vacancy, or hole, in the copper 3d-electron shell, which can contain up to 10 electrons. The ion {{bracket|Cu(H<sub>2</sub>O)<sub>6</sub>}}<sup>2+</sup> is a typical example of a compound with this characteristic.
# Six-coordinate complexes of the Cu(II) ion, with the generic formula [CuL<sub>6</sub>]<sup>2+</sup>, are subject to the [[Jahn–Teller effect]] so that the symmetry is reduced from octahedral (point group O<sub>h</sub>) to tetragonal (point group D<sub>4h</sub>). Since d orbitals are centrosymmetric the related atomic term symbols can be classified in the [[subgroup]] D<sub>4</sub>.
# To a first approximation [[spin–orbit coupling]] can be ignored and the magnetic moment is then predicted to be {{val|1.73|u=[[Bohr magneton|''μ''<sub>B</sub>]]}}, the so-called spin-only value. However, for a more accurate prediction spin–orbit coupling must be taken into consideration. This means that the relevant quantum number is {{math|''J''}}, where {{math|1=''J'' = ''L'' + ''S''}}. 
# When ''J'' is half-integer, the ''character'' for a rotation by an angle of {{math|''α'' + 2''π''}} [[radian]]s is equal to minus the ''character'' for rotation by an angle {{math|''α''}}. This cannot be true for an identity in a point group. Consequently, a group must be used in which rotations by {{math|''α'' + 2''π''}} are classed as symmetry operations distinct from rotations by an angle {{math|''α''}}. This group is known as the double group, D<sub>4</sub>′.

With species such as the square-planar complex of the [[silver]](II) ion [AgF<sub>4</sub>]<sup>2−</sup> the relevant double group is also D<sub>4</sub>′; deviations from the spin-only value are greater as the magnitude of spin–orbit coupling is greater for silver(II) than for copper(II).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Foëx |first1=D. |last2=Gorter |first2=C. J. |last3=Smits |first3=L.J. |title=Constantes Sélectionées Diamagnetism et Paramagnetism |date=1957 |publisher=Masson et Cie|location=Paris}}</ref>

A double group is also used for some compounds of [[titanium]] in the +3 oxidation state. Compounds of titanium(III) have a single electron in the 3d shell. The magnetic moments of octahedral complexes with the generic formula [TiL<sub>6</sub>]<sup>''n''+</sup> have been found to lie in the range 1.63–1.81&nbsp;B.M. at room temperature.<ref name=GE>{{Greenwood&Earnshaw2nd|page=971}}</ref> The double group O′ is used to classify their electronic states.

The [[cerium]](III) ion, Ce<sup>3+</sup>, has a single electron in the 4f shell. The magnetic properties of octahedral complexes of this ion are treated using the double group O′.

When a cerium(III) ion is encapsulated in a C<sub>60</sub> cage, the formula  of the [[endohedral fullerene]] is written as {{brace|Ce<sup>3+</sup>@C<sub>60</sub><sup>3−</sup>}}.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chai |first1=Yan |last2=Guo |first2=Ting |last3=Jin |first3=Changming |last4=Haufler |first4=Robert E. |last5=Chibante |first5=L. P. Felipe |last6=Fure |first6=Jan |last7=Wang |first7=Lihong |last8=Alford |first8=J. Michael |last9=Smalley |first9=Richard E. |title=Fullerenes with metals inside |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry |date=1991 |volume=95 |issue=20 |pages=7564–7568 |doi=10.1021/j100173a002}}</ref>

=== Free radicals ===
Double groups may be used in connection with [[free radicals]]. This has been illustrated for the species CH<sub>3</sub>F<sup>+</sup> and CH<sub>3</sub>BF<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> which both contain a single unpaired electron.<ref>{{citation |last1=Bunker |first1=P.R. |editor1-last= Hinze |editor1-first=J. |chapter=The Spin Double Groups of Molecular Symmetry Groups|date=1979 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-93124-6_4|title=The Permutation Group in Physics and Chemistry|volume=12|series= Lecture Notes in Chemistry|publisher= [[Springer-Verlag|Springer]]|pages=38–56|isbn= 978-3-540-09707-5}}</ref>
